hints: Notice the four options pair two numerators, energy and power, with two denominators, charge and current, and p.d. is measured in volts.
Recall $V = W/Q$ where $W$ is energy transferred in $\text{J}$ and $Q$ is charge in $\text{C}$, so $1 \text{ V} = 1 \text{ J C}^{-1}$.
Check the other pairings using $P = W/t$ and $I = Q/t$ to see why energy per current and power per charge do not give $\text{J C}^{-1}$.
walkthrough: Identify what is asked: the formal definition of p.d. across a component, not a rearranged formula that happens to equal volts.
State the governing relation: $V = W/Q$, where $V$ is potential difference, $W$ is energy transferred from electrical to other forms, and $Q$ is charge moved.
Check units: $W$ in $\text{J}$ divided by $Q$ in $\text{C}$ gives $\text{J C}^{-1}$, which is the volt $\text{V}$.
Compare options: only energy per unit charge matches $W/Q$ directly, while energy per current adds an extra time factor and power per charge introduces rate incorrectly.
Note that power per unit current equals $VI/I = V$ in value because $P = VI$, but it is a derived result, not the definition in terms of energy and charge.
Therefore the definition is energy transferred per unit charge. This is option A

options.A: The p.d. is defined by $V = W/Q$, the electrical energy $W$ transferred per unit charge $Q$ passing through the component.
options.B: Energy per unit current is $W/I$, which has unit $\text{J A}^{-1}$ or $\text{V s}$, not volts.
options.C: Power $P$ is rate of energy transfer, so power per unit charge $P/Q$ does not give $V = W/Q$.
options.D: Although $P/I = V$ numerically from $P = VI$, the definition of p.d. is stated with energy and charge, not power and current.
